content: Nisin is a polycyclic peptide with antibacterial properties, composed of 34 amino acid residues. It is commonly used as a food preservative. The molecule contains several uncommon amino acids, including lanthionine (Lan), methyllanthionine (MeLan), dehydroalanine (Dha), and dehydroaminobutyric acid (Dhb). These unusual amino acids are introduced through post-translational modifications of the precursor peptide. During these reactions, a ribosomally synthesized 57-mer precursor peptide is enzymatically converted into the final active peptide. The unsaturated amino acids in nisin are derived from serine and threonine residues. The addition of cysteine residues to the dehydro amino acids, catalyzed by specific enzymes, results in the formation of multiple thioether bridges, which contribute to the molecule's stability and bioactivity. Nisin is produced through fermentation by the bacterium Lactococcus lactis. Commercially, it is obtained from natural substrates such as milk and is not chemically synthesized. It is widely used in the production of processed cheese to extend shelf life by inhibiting the growth of gram-positive spoilage and pathogenic bacteria. Beyond cheese production, nisin has numerous applications in the food and beverage industry as a preservative. Due to its highly selective spectrum of antimicrobial activity, nisin is also employed as a selective agent in microbiological media to isolate gram-negative bacteria, yeasts, and molds. Nisin is structurally related to other molecules such as subtilin and epidermin, all of which belong to a class of antimicrobial peptides known as lantibiotics. As a food additive, nisin is designated with the E number E234.
